Slides accessible here: `https://pengyunc.quarto.pub/week10/` ## This tutorial: Prediction Interval Estimation {auto-animate="true"} In this tutorial we use simulation to understand and explore the methods for prediction interval calculation.
:::{.callout-note title="Activities"} - Exercises 1 & 2: Simulating 95% prediction intervals — coverage and average length (width) - Exercise 3: Investigating the effect of model misspecification on prediction interval properties - Exercise 4: Simulating prediction intervals with non-normal disturbances ::: ## Recap: Prediction Intervals {auto-animate="true"} :::{.fragment} - Consider an AR(1) model and assume $Y_{n+1}$ has conditional distribution: $$ Y_{n+1} = \phi_{1}Y_{n} + U_{n+1} \quad \text{and} \quad Y_{n+1}\mid \mathscr{Y}_{t} \sim \mathrm{N}(\phi_{1}Y_{n}, \sigma_{n}^{2}) $$ $$ \color{blue}{\implies\quad \sigma_{n}^{2}=\operatorname{var}(Y_{n+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{n}) = \operatorname{var}(U_{n+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{n})} $$ where $U_{t+1}$ is the 1-step-ahead prediction error. ::: :::{.fragment} - The 95% confidence interval for $(Y_{n+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{n})$ is: $$\phi_{1}Y_{n}\pm 1.96\times \sigma_{n}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} - It follows that the 95\% prediction interval for $Y_{n+1}$ is: $$\quad\quad\color{purple}{\hat{\phi}_{1}}Y_{t}\color{black}{\,\pm\, 1.96\times\,}\color{teal}{\hat{\sigma}_{n}}\color{black}\quad\text{where}\quad \begin{aligned}\color{purple}{\hat{\phi}_{1}}&\color{purple}{\text{ is the usual parameter estimate}}\\ \color{teal}{\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{n}}&\color{teal}{=\frac{1}{n}\sum^{n}_{t=2}\hat{U}_{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}$$ assuming $\operatorname{var}(U_{t}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t-1})$ is constant for all $t$. ::: ## Recap: Prediction Intervals {auto-animate="true"} - It follows that the 95\% prediction interval for $Y_{n+1}$ is: $$\quad\quad\color{purple}{\hat{\phi}_{1}}Y_{n}\color{black}{\,\pm\, 1.96\times\,}\color{teal}{\hat{\sigma}_{n}}\color{black}\quad\text{where}\quad \begin{aligned}\color{purple}{\hat{\phi}_{1}}&\color{purple}{\text{ is the usual parameter estimate}}\\ \color{teal}{\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{n}}&\color{teal}{=\frac{1}{n}\sum^{n}_{t=2}\hat{U}_{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}$$ assuming $\operatorname{var}(U_{t}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t-1})$ is constant for all $t$. :::{.fragment} - This prediction interval contains $Y_{n+1}$ with approximately 95% probability in repeated samples. $\to$ we will illustrate this with a simulation ::: :::{.fragment} - This probability is understood in the frequentist sense: - given repeated drawings from the “population” of the data, the proportion of the constructed intervals will include actual $Y_t$ is 95%. ::: :::{.fragment} - Precision: A narrower prediction interval indicates a more precise forecast. ::: ## Exercises 1 and 2 {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Simulate the 95% prediction intervals for $Y_{t+h}$ for $h=1,\dots,12$ for the AR process: $$Y_{t}=0.8Y_{t-1}+U_{t}\quad\text{where}\quad U_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1)$$ Include in the simulation a calculation for the average length of the PIs for each $h$. :::
:::{.callout-tip title="Code Outline"} :::{.incremental} - Repeat the following experiment `reps=1000` times: - Generate $200+12$ draws of $U_t$ from $\mathrm{N}(0,1)$ - Simulate $200+12$ observations from the AR(1) process - Withhold the final 12 observations as test set - Estimate the AR(1) model with the training set - Compute and store the upper and lower bounds of 95% PI for $h=1,2,\dots,12$ - Check whether the true values are contained within the 95% PIs - **Exercise 1:** Compute the probability at which the 95% PIs contains the true $Y_{t+h}$ for $h=1,2,\dots,12$ - **Exercise 2:** Compute the average lengths of the 95% PIs for each $h=1,2,\dots,12$ ::: ::: ## Exercises 1 and 2 {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Simulate the 95% prediction intervals for $Y_{t+h}$ for $h=1,\dots,12$ for the AR process: $$Y_{t}=0.8Y_{t-1}+U_{t}\quad\text{where}\quad U_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1)$$ Include in the simulation a calculation for the average length of the PIs for each $h$. :::
:::{.panel-tabset} ## Initialisation ```{r} library(forecast) set.seed(30004) # For reproducibility reps <- 1000 n <- 200 # Estimation sample size per experiment hmax <- 12 # Forecast horizon ar <- 0.8 # AR(1) true coefficient # Storage for inclusion indicators Included <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=hmax) # Storage for length of each interval Length <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=hmax) ``` ## Simulation ```{r} for (r in 1:reps){ U <- rnorm(n+hmax) # N(0,1) prediction errors Y <- arima.sim(n=n+hmax, model=list(ar=ar), innov=U) # Simulate data Yf <- Y[(n+1):(n+hmax)] # Forecast sample Y <- Y[1:n] # Estimation sample # Estimate AR(1) model and generate forecasts and PIs eq <- Arima(Y, order=c(1,0,0)) eqf <- forecast(eq, h=hmax) Lower <- eqf$lower[,"95%"] # lower bound of 95% PIs Upper <- eqf$upper[,"95%"] # upper bound of 95% PIs Included[r,] <- 1*(LowerYf) # Check inclusion Length[r,] <- Upper-Lower # Lengths of PIs } ``` ## Extracting PIs Explained ```{r} eqf <- forecast(eq, h=hmax) print(eqf) ```
```{r} # Extract the lower bounds for 95% PI for h=1,2,...,12 print(eqf$lower) # eqf$lower[,"95%"] ``` ## Results ```{r} # Record 1 if true value contained within 95% PI, 0 otherwise print(head(Included)) # Recorded as difference between upper and lower bounds of 95% PI print(head(Length)) ``` ::: ## Exercises 1 and 2 {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Simulate the 95% prediction intervals for $Y_{t+h}$ for $h=1,\dots,12$ for the AR process: $$Y_{t}=0.8Y_{t-1}+U_{t}\quad\text{where}\quad U_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1)$$ Include in the simulation a calculation for the average length of the PIs for each $h$. :::
:::{.panel-tabset} ## Exercise 1 - Coverage :::{.callout-question} Compute the probabilities at which the 95% PIs contains the true $Y_{t+h}$ for $h=1,\dots,12$. :::
```{r} Coverage <- apply(Included, 2, mean) * 100 names(Coverage) <- paste0("h=", 1:hmax) print(Coverage) ```
The simulated coverages are slightly below 95%? - arises partly because of simulation error (only 1000 simulations) - also partly because the forecast intervals are based on model estimates from $n=200$ sample sizes which do not yield the exact model coefficients. ## Exercise 2 - Lengths :::{.callout-question} Compute the average lengths of the 95% PIs for each $h=1,2,\dots,12$. :::
```{r} AvgLength <- round(apply(Length, 2, mean), 2) names(AvgLength) <- paste0("h=", 1:hmax) print(AvgLength) ```
- The average length of the interval is increasing in $h$, which reflects the formula we have seen in lectures for the variances for $h$-step-ahead forecasts. $$\textstyle\operatorname{var}(U_{t\mid t-h})=\sum^{h-1}_{j=0}\phi_{1}^{2j}\sigma^{2}\qquad\color{teal}{\boxed{\leftarrow\;\textsf{\small{}From Lecture 9}\;}}$$ - Intuition: it is *more difficult* to forecast further into the future. ::: ## Exercise 3 {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Now change the simulation to demonstrate the effects of model misspecification on the properties of the prediction intervals. $\to$ **Simulate AR(1) data, but forecast with MA(1)** What are the implications for the prediction intervals? Explain the results for the lengths of the prediction intervals for $h>1$. ::: :::{.panel-tabset} ## Initialisation Code Code for initialisation is the same as in Exercises 1 and 2. ```{r} set.seed(30004) # For reproducibility reps <- 1000 n <- 200 # Estimation sample size per experiment hmax <- 12 # Forecast horizon ar <- 0.8 # AR(1) true coefficient # Storage for inclusion indicators Included <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=hmax) # Storage for length of each interval Length <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=hmax) ``` ## Estimation Code The only change is to the estimation command, replacing AR(1) with MA(1). ```{r} for (r in 1:reps){ U <- rnorm(n+hmax) # N(0,1) prediction errors Y <- arima.sim(n=n+hmax, model=list(ar=ar), innov=U) # Simulate data Yf <- Y[(n+1):(n+hmax)] # Forecast sample Y <- Y[1:n] # Estimation sample # Estimate MA(1) model and generate forecasts and PIs eq <- Arima(Y, order=c(0,0,1)) ### <- MISSPECIFIED!!! eqf <- forecast(eq, h=hmax) Lower <- eqf$lower[,"95%"] # lower bound of 95% PIs Upper <- eqf$upper[,"95%"] # upper bound of 95% PIs Included[r,] <- 1*(LowerYf) # Check inclusion Length[r,] <- Upper-Lower # Lengths of PIs } ```
## Results: Coverage ```{r} # Coverage: proportion of inclusion at each h Coverage <- apply(Included, 2, mean)*100 names(Coverage) <- paste0("h=",1:hmax) print(Coverage) ```
When the model is misspecified: - the coverage rates of the prediction intervals decrease below 90% as $h$ increases. - the true value is included within the interval less frequently than the desired 90%. ## Results: Lengths ```{r} # Average interval lengths: AvgLength <- round(apply(Length, 2, mean),2) names(AvgLength) <- paste0("h=",1:hmax) print(AvgLength) ```
The average lengths of the 95% PIs are the same for $h=2,\dots,12$. ::: ## Exercise 3 {auto-animate="true"} **What's going on?** ```{r echo=FALSE} # Average interval lengths: AvgLength <- round(apply(Length, 2, mean),2) names(AvgLength) <- paste0("h=",1:hmax) print(AvgLength) ```
:::{.fragment} :::{.callout-tip} Consider the MA(1) model: for any $t$ we have $$Y_{t}=U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}\quad\text{where}\quad U_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$$ To compute the 95% PI for $Y_{t+h}$, we need to know the distribution for $Y_{t+h}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}.$ ::: :::
:::{.fragment} When $h=1$: $$Y_{t+1}=U_{t+1}+\theta_{1}U_{t}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} $$\implies\quad \mathbb{E}(Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}(U_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=\mathbb{E}(U_{t+1})=0}+\theta_{1}\underbrace{\mathbb{E}(U_{t}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=u_t}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} $$\implies\quad \mathbb{E}(Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\theta_{1}u_{t}$$ where $u_{t}$ is the realised value of $U_t$ (it is a constant). ::: ## Exercise 3 {auto-animate="true"} **What's going on?** ```{r echo=FALSE} # Average interval lengths: AvgLength <- round(apply(Length, 2, mean),2) names(AvgLength) <- paste0("h=",1:hmax) print(AvgLength) ```
:::{.callout-tip} Consider the MA(1) model: for any $t$ we have $$Y_{t}=U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}\quad\text{where}\quad U_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$$ To compute the 95% PI for $Y_{t+h}$, we need to know the distribution for $Y_{t+h}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}.$ :::
When $h=1$: Mean of $Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}$: $\mathbb{E}(Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\theta_{1}u_{t}$. :::{.fragment}
How about the variance? ::: :::{.center} [$\displaystyle\operatorname{var}(Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\underbrace{\operatorname{var}(U_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=\operatorname{var}(U_{t+1})=\sigma^{2}}+\underbrace{\;\;\operatorname{var}(\theta_{1}U_{t}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})\;\;}_{=0,\; \theta_{1}u_{t}\text{ is a constant}}$]{.fragment}[$=\sigma^{2}$]{.fragment} ::: ## Exercise 3 {auto-animate="true"} **What's going on?** ```{r echo=FALSE} # Average interval lengths: AvgLength <- round(apply(Length, 2, mean),2) names(AvgLength) <- paste0("h=",1:hmax) print(AvgLength) ```
:::{.callout-tip} Consider the MA(1) model: for any $t$ we have $$Y_{t}=U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}\quad\text{where}\quad U_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$$ To compute the 95% PI for $Y_{t+h}$, we need to know the distribution for $Y_{t+h}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}.$ :::
When $h=1$: Mean of $Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}$: $\mathbb{E}(Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\theta_{1}u_{t}$. Variance of $Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}$: $\operatorname{var}(Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\sigma^{2}$ :::{.fragment}
Given that $Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}=U_{t+1}+\theta_{1}u_{t}$ and $U_{t+1}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$, ::: :::{.center} [$\implies Y_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(\theta_{1}u_{t},\sigma^{2})\quad$]{.fragment} [$\color{teal}{\implies \textsf{the 95\% PI is}\quad \hat{\theta}_{1}u_{t}\pm 1.96\hat{\sigma}}$]{.fragment} ::: ## Exercise 3 {auto-animate="true"} **What's going on?** ```{r echo=FALSE} # Average interval lengths: AvgLength <- round(apply(Length, 2, mean),2) names(AvgLength) <- paste0("h=",1:hmax) print(AvgLength) ```
:::{.callout-tip} Consider the MA(1) model: for any $t$ we have $$Y_{t}=U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}\quad\text{where}\quad U_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$$ To compute the 95% PI for $Y_{t+h}$, we need to know the distribution for $Y_{t+h}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}.$ :::
When $h=1$, the 95% prediction interval is $\hat{\theta}_{1}u_{t}\pm 1.96\hat{\sigma}$. [When $h=2$,]{.fragment} [we have $Y_{t+2}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}=U_{t+2}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}$.]{.fragment} :::{.incremental} - **Mean:** $\;\;\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(Y_{t+2}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}(U_{t+2}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=\mathbb{E}(U_{t+2})=0}+\theta_{1}\underbrace{\mathbb{E}(U_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=\mathbb{E}(U_{t+1})=0}=0$ - **Variance:** $\;\;\displaystyle\mathrm{var}(Y_{t+2}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})=\underbrace{\mathrm{var}(U_{t+2}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=\operatorname{var}(U_{t+2})=\sigma^{2}}+\underbrace{\mathrm{var}(\theta_{1}U_{t+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t})}_{=\theta_{1}^{2}\operatorname{var}(U_{t+1})=\theta_{1}^{2}\sigma^{2}}=(1+\theta_{1}^{2})\sigma^{2}$ - **95% PI:** $\;\;$Since $Y_{t+2}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,(1+\theta_{1}^{2})\sigma^{2})\;\;\implies\;\; 0\pm1.96\times \sqrt{(1+\hat{\theta}_{1}^{2})\hat{\sigma}^{2}}$

The normal and bootstrap prediction intervals will be compared. (a) The first distribution for $U_t$ is the $\chi_{1}^{2}$ (i.e. chi-squared with 1 degree of freedom) centered to have mean 0. ::: :::{.panel-tabset} ## True DGP - We know that when $X\sim\chi_{k}^{2}$, $\mathbb{E}(X)=k$ and $\operatorname{var}(X)=2k$. - To standardise it (mean 0 and unit variance), we can take the "z-score": $$U=\frac{X-\mathbb{E}(X)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{var}(X)}}=\frac{X-1}{\sqrt{2}}$$ - The true DGP is: $$Y_{t}=\phi_{1}Y_{t-1}+U_{t}\quad\textsf{where}\quad \color{blue}{\underbrace{\;\;U_{t}=\frac{X-1}{\sqrt{2}}\quad\textsf{and}\quad X\sim\chi_{1}^{2}\;\;}_{\chi^{2}_{1}\textsf{ centered to have mean 0}}}$$ ## PDF Shape ```{r} x <- seq(-1, 5, length.out = 500) # support starts at -1 y <- dchisq(x + 1, df = 1) # density of χ²(1), shifted plot(x, y, type = "l", col = "red", lwd = 2, main = "", ylab = "", xlab = "", ylim = c(0, 1.5)) abline(h = 0, lty = 2) # horizontal line at 0 ``` ## Full Code The following code took me around 27 minutes and 10 seconds to run (on a 2025 MacBook Pro, 5 minutes slower than David's "unremarkable 2011 MacBook Pro").
```{r eval=FALSE} library(forecast) reps <- 1000 n <- 200 h <- 12 arv <- c(0.3,0.6,0.9) Coverage <- matrix(nrow=length(arv), ncol=h) colnames(Coverage) <- paste0("h=",1:h) rownames(Coverage) <- paste0("ar=",arv) CoverageBS <- Coverage AvgLength <- Coverage AvgLengthBS <- Coverage et<- system.time( for (ac in 1:length(arv)){ ar <- arv[ac] Included <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) IncludedBS <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) Length <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) LengthBS <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) set.seed(3400) for (r in 1:reps){ # Simulate time series U <- ((rnorm(n+h))^2-1)/sqrt(2) Y <- arima.sim(n=n+h, model=list(ar=ar), innov=U) Yf <- Y[(n+1):(n+h)] Y <- Y[1:n] # AR(1) estimation eq <- Arima(Y, order=c(1,0,0)) # Normal prediction interval eqf <- forecast(eq, h=h) Lower <- eqf$lower[,"95%"] Upper <- eqf$upper[,"95%"] Included[r,] <- 1*(LowerYf) Length[r,] <- Upper-Lower # Bootstrap prediction interval eqf <- forecast(eq, h=h, bootstrap=TRUE) LowerBS <- eqf$lower[,"95%"] UpperBS <- eqf$upper[,"95%"] IncludedBS[r,] <- 1*(LowerBSYf) LengthBS[r,] <- UpperBS-LowerBS } Coverage[ac,] <- apply(Included, 2, mean)*100 CoverageBS[ac,] <- apply(IncludedBS, 2, mean)*100 AvgLength[ac,] <- round(apply(Length, 2, mean),2) AvgLengthBS[ac,] <- round(apply(LengthBS, 2, mean),2) }) ```
## Result - Coverage ```{r echo=FALSE} # Coverage Coverage <- matrix( c( 95,94.4,92.8,93.4,94.9,96.0,94.9,95.0,93.3,94.0,94.2,94.7, 94,94.4,94.4,94.2,94.2,94.3,94.3,94.6,95.4,94.3,96.0,95.1, 94,93.9,93.2,94.3,93.0,94.8,93.8,94.4,93.7,94.4,93.2,93.6 ), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list( c("ar=0.3", "ar=0.6", "ar=0.9"), paste0("h=", 1:12) ) ) # CoverageBS CoverageBS <- matrix( c( 94.5,93.3,93.8,93.4,95.5,95.3,94.7,93.4,93.0,94.4,94.5,94.0, 94.3,93.1,93.9,93.9,92.6,92.5,93.2,93.6,94.6,94.0,93.7,92.4, 93.5,92.5,92.2,92.9,92.0,92.9,91.8,92.1,91.3,93.0,92.6,93.4 ), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list( c("ar=0.3", "ar=0.6", "ar=0.9"), paste0("h=", 1:12) ) ) ``` ```{r} print(Coverage) # Normal Assumption (Misspecified) print(CoverageBS) # Bootstrapped ```
- The coverage results are very similar across the boards. - Note: Remember these are just simulation estimates from only 1000 replications, and don't over-interpret small differences. - Nevertheless there might be a slight deficiency of about 1% in the coverage of the bootstrap intervals relative to the normal intervals when $\phi=0.9$. - Otherwise, there is little to choose between the two intervals on this criterion. - This is quite interesting because theoretically the bootstrap intervals are valid in this case but the normal intervals are not. - Note: CLT does not provide an approximation for non-normal data when computing prediction intervals. ## Result - Lengths ```{r echo=FALSE} # AvgLength AvgLength <- matrix( c( 3.90,4.06,4.08,4.08,4.08,4.08,4.08,4.08,4.08,4.08,4.08,4.08, 3.91,4.54,4.75,4.82,4.85,4.86,4.86,4.87,4.87,4.87,4.87,4.87, 3.91,5.22,6.05,6.64,7.07,7.39,7.64,7.83,7.98,8.10,8.20,8.27 ), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list( c("ar=0.3", "ar=0.6", "ar=0.9"), paste0("h=", 1:12) ) ) # AvgLengthBS AvgLengthBS <- matrix( c( 3.61,3.81,3.86,3.86,3.87,3.85,3.86,3.87,3.86,3.86,3.86,3.86, 3.62,4.28,4.53,4.63,4.66,4.68,4.69,4.70,4.69,4.69,4.70,4.70, 3.62,4.93,5.80,6.41,6.86,7.19,7.45,7.65,7.82,7.94,8.04,8.13 ), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list( c("ar=0.3", "ar=0.6", "ar=0.9"), paste0("h=", 1:12) ) ) ``` ```{r} print(AvgLength) # Normal Assumption (Misspecified) print(AvgLengthBS) # Bootstrapped ```
The bootstrap intervals can be as much as 10% shorter for small $h$, although this advantage reduces to 5% or less as $h$ increases. ::: ## Exercise 4(a) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Next we well consider the properties of prediction intervals when the normality assumption is not correct. The normal and bootstrap prediction intervals will be compared. (a) The first distribution for $U_t$ is the $\chi_{1}^{2}$ (i.e. chi-squared with 1 degree of freedom) centered to have mean 0. :::

The normal and bootstrap prediction intervals will be compared. The normal and bootstrap prediction intervals will be compared. (a) The first distribution for $U_t$ is the $\chi_{1}^{2}$ (i.e. chi-squared with 1 degree of freedom) centered to have mean 0. ::: :::{.panel-tabset} ## True DGP - We know that when $X\sim\chi_{k}^{2}$, $\mathbb{E}(X)=k$ and $\operatorname{var}(X)=2k$. - To standardise it (mean 0 and unit variance), we can take the "z-score": $$U=\frac{X-\mathbb{E}(X)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{var}(X)}}=\frac{X-1}{\sqrt{2}}$$ - The true DGP is: $$Y_{t}=\phi_{1}Y_{t-1}+U_{t}\quad\textsf{where}\quad \color{blue}{\underbrace{\;\;U_{t}=\frac{X-1}{\sqrt{2}}\quad\textsf{and}\quad X\sim\chi_{1}^{2}\;\;}_{\chi^{2}_{1}\textsf{ centered to have mean 0}}}$$ ## PDF Shape ```{r} x <- seq(-1, 5, length.out = 500) # support starts at -1 y <- dchisq(x + 1, df = 1) # density of χ²(1), shifted plot(x, y, type = "l", col = "red", lwd = 2, main = "", ylab = "", xlab = "", ylim = c(0, 1.5)) abline(h = 0, lty = 2) # horizontal line at 0 ``` ## Full Code The following code took me around 27 minutes and 10 seconds to run (on a 2025 MacBook Pro, 5 minutes slower than David's "unremarkable 2011 MacBook Pro").
```{r eval=FALSE} library(forecast) reps <- 1000 n <- 200 h <- 12 arv <- c(0.3,0.6,0.9) Coverage <- matrix(nrow=length(arv), ncol=h) colnames(Coverage) <- paste0("h=",1:h) rownames(Coverage) <- paste0("ar=",arv) CoverageBS <- Coverage AvgLength <- Coverage AvgLengthBS <- Coverage et<- system.time( for (ac in 1:length(arv)){ ar <- arv[ac] Included <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) IncludedBS <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) Length <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) LengthBS <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) set.seed(3400) for (r in 1:reps){ # Simulate time series U <- ((rnorm(n+h))^2-1)/sqrt(2) Y <- arima.sim(n=n+h, model=list(ar=ar), innov=U) Yf <- Y[(n+1):(n+h)] Y <- Y[1:n] # AR(1) estimation eq <- Arima(Y, order=c(1,0,0)) # Normal prediction interval eqf <- forecast(eq, h=h) Lower <- eqf$lower[,"95%"] Upper <- eqf$upper[,"95%"] Included[r,] <- 1*(LowerYf) Length[r,] <- Upper-Lower # Bootstrap prediction interval eqf <- forecast(eq, h=h, bootstrap=TRUE) LowerBS <- eqf$lower[,"95%"] UpperBS <- eqf$upper[,"95%"] IncludedBS[r,] <- 1*(LowerBSYf) LengthBS[r,] <- UpperBS-LowerBS } Coverage[ac,] <- apply(Included, 2, mean)*100 CoverageBS[ac,] <- apply(IncludedBS, 2, mean)*100 AvgLength[ac,] <- round(apply(Length, 2, mean),2) AvgLengthBS[ac,] <- round(apply(LengthBS, 2, mean),2) }) ```
## Result - Coverage ```{r echo=FALSE} # Coverage Coverage <- matrix( c( 95,94.4,92.8,93.4,94.9,96.0,94.9,95.0,93.3,94.0,94.2,94.7, 94,94.4,94.4,94.2,94.2,94.3,94.3,94.6,95.4,94.3,96.0,95.1, 94,93.9,93.2,94.3,93.0,94.8,93.8,94.4,93.7,94.4,93.2,93.6 ), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list( c("ar=0.3", "ar=0.6", "ar=0.9"), paste0("h=", 1:12) ) ) # CoverageBS CoverageBS <- matrix( c( 94.5,93.3,93.8,93.4,95.5,95.3,94.7,93.4,93.0,94.4,94.5,94.0, 94.3,93.1,93.9,93.9,92.6,92.5,93.2,93.6,94.6,94.0,93.7,92.4, 93.5,92.5,92.2,92.9,92.0,92.9,91.8,92.1,91.3,93.0,92.6,93.4 ), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list( c("ar=0.3", "ar=0.6", "ar=0.9"), paste0("h=", 1:12) ) ) ``` ```{r} print(Coverage) # Normal Assumption (Misspecified) print(CoverageBS) # Bootstrapped ```
- The coverage results are very similar across the boards. - Note: Remember these are just simulation estimates from only 1000 replications, and don't over-interpret small differences. - Nevertheless there might be a slight deficiency of about 1% in the coverage of the bootstrap intervals relative to the normal intervals when $\phi=0.9$. - Otherwise, there is little to choose between the two intervals on this criterion. - This is quite interesting because theoretically the bootstrap intervals are valid in this case but the normal intervals are not. - Note: CLT does not provide an approximation for non-normal data when computing prediction intervals. ## Result - Lengths ```{r echo=FALSE} # AvgLength AvgLength <- matrix( c( 3.90,4.06,4.08,4.08,4.08,4.08,4.08,4.08,4.08,4.08,4.08,4.08, 3.91,4.54,4.75,4.82,4.85,4.86,4.86,4.87,4.87,4.87,4.87,4.87, 3.91,5.22,6.05,6.64,7.07,7.39,7.64,7.83,7.98,8.10,8.20,8.27 ), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list( c("ar=0.3", "ar=0.6", "ar=0.9"), paste0("h=", 1:12) ) ) # AvgLengthBS AvgLengthBS <- matrix( c( 3.61,3.81,3.86,3.86,3.87,3.85,3.86,3.87,3.86,3.86,3.86,3.86, 3.62,4.28,4.53,4.63,4.66,4.68,4.69,4.70,4.69,4.69,4.70,4.70, 3.62,4.93,5.80,6.41,6.86,7.19,7.45,7.65,7.82,7.94,8.04,8.13 ), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list( c("ar=0.3", "ar=0.6", "ar=0.9"), paste0("h=", 1:12) ) ) ``` ```{r} print(AvgLength) # Normal Assumption (Misspecified) print(AvgLengthBS) # Bootstrapped ```
The bootstrap intervals can be as much as 10% shorter for small $h$, although this advantage reduces to 5% or less as $h$ increases. ::: ## Exercise 4(a) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Next we well consider the properties of prediction intervals when the normality assumption is not correct. The normal and bootstrap prediction intervals will be compared. (a) The first distribution for $U_t$ is the $\chi_{1}^{2}$ (i.e. chi-squared with 1 degree of freedom) centered to have mean 0. :::
**Overall:** :::{.incremental} - There are not major differences between the two intervals and the choice would be subjective. - The advantage in length may suggest some *weak preference* for the bootstrap intervals in this particular model. ::: ## Exercise 4(b) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Next we well consider the properties of prediction intervals when the normality assumption is not correct. The normal and bootstrap prediction intervals will be compared. (b) The second distribution for $U_t$ is the $t$ distribution with 4 degrees of freedom. ::: :::{.panel-tabset} ## True DGP The true DGP is: $$Y_{t}=\phi_{1}Y_{t-1}+U_{t}\quad\textsf{where}\quad \color{blue}{U_{t}\sim t_{4}}$$ This distribution has fatter tails (higher kurtosis) than $\mathrm{N}(0,1)$: ```{r} x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1000) y_t <- dt(x, df = 4) y_norm <- dnorm(x) plot(x, y_t, type = "l", col = "red", lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 0.45), ylab = "", xlab = "", main = "") lines(x, y_norm, col = "blue", lty = 2, lwd = 2) abline(h = 0, lty = 3) legend("topright", legend = c("t (df=4)", "Normal(0,1)"), col = c("red", "blue"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2) ``` ## Full Code ```{r eval=FALSE} library(forecast) reps <- 1000 n <- 200 h <- 12 arv <- c(0.3,0.6,0.9) Coverage <- matrix(nrow=length(arv), ncol=h) colnames(Coverage) <- paste0("h=",1:h) rownames(Coverage) <- paste0("ar=",arv) CoverageBS <- Coverage AvgLength <- Coverage AvgLengthBS <- Coverage et<- system.time( for (ac in 1:length(arv)){ ar <- arv[ac] Included <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) IncludedBS <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) Length <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) LengthBS <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=h) set.seed(3400) for (r in 1:reps){ # Simulate time series U <- rt(n=n+h, df=4) Y <- arima.sim(n=n+h, model=list(ar=ar), innov=U) Yf <- Y[(n+1):(n+h)] Y <- Y[1:n] # AR(1) estimation eq <- Arima(Y, order=c(1,0,0)) # Normal prediction interval eqf <- forecast(eq, h=h) Lower <- eqf$lower[,"95%"] Upper <- eqf$upper[,"95%"] Included[r,] <- 1*(LowerYf) Length[r,] <- Upper-Lower # Bootstrap prediction interval eqf <- forecast(eq, h=h, bootstrap=TRUE) LowerBS <- eqf$lower[,"95%"] UpperBS <- eqf$upper[,"95%"] IncludedBS[r,] <- 1*(LowerBSYf) LengthBS[r,] <- UpperBS-LowerBS } Coverage[ac,] <- apply(Included, 2, mean)*100 CoverageBS[ac,] <- apply(IncludedBS, 2, mean)*100 AvgLength[ac,] <- round(apply(Length, 2, mean),2) AvgLengthBS[ac,] <- round(apply(LengthBS, 2, mean),2) }) ```
```{r echo=FALSE} # Normal PI coverage Coverage_normal <- matrix( c( 94.9,95.0,94.8,94.0,94.6,94.8,93.3,94.0,94.5,94.4,95.9,94.2, 95.2,93.8,94.2,93.6,92.1,94.5,95.2,94.0,94.0,94.9,93.6,93.5, 94.6,95.4,93.7,93.4,93.4,93.4,93.4,91.3,91.5,90.8,91.0,90.8 ), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE ) colnames(Coverage_normal) <- paste0("h=",1:12) rownames(Coverage_normal) <- c("ar=0.3","ar=0.6","ar=0.9") Coverage <- Coverage_normal # Bootstrap PI coverage Coverage_bootstrap <- matrix( c( 94.8,94.6,95.0,94.1,94.3,94.8,93.5,94.2,94.3,94.5,95.4,93.6, 95.7,94.3,93.5,93.4,92.5,94.4,95.3,94.2,93.7,94.6,93.3,93.9, 94.2,95.4,93.8,93.7,92.9,93.1,93.0,91.1,91.3,90.2,90.4,90.1 ), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE ) colnames(Coverage_bootstrap) <- paste0("h=",1:12) rownames(Coverage_bootstrap) <- c("ar=0.3","ar=0.6","ar=0.9") CoverageBS <- Coverage_bootstrap # Normal PI average length AvgLength_normal <- matrix( c( 5.48,5.71,5.73,5.74,5.74,5.74,5.74,5.74,5.74,5.74,5.74,5.74, 5.45,6.32,6.60,6.70,6.74,6.76,6.76,6.76,6.77,6.77,6.77,6.77, 5.52,7.35,8.50,9.31,9.89,10.33,10.66,10.92,11.12,11.28,11.40,11.50 ), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE ) colnames(AvgLength_normal) <- paste0("h=",1:12) rownames(AvgLength_normal) <- c("ar=0.3","ar=0.6","ar=0.9") AvgLength <- AvgLength_normal # Bootstrap PI average length AvgLength_bootstrap <- matrix( c( 5.54,5.77,5.80,5.80,5.79,5.81,5.79,5.80,5.80,5.80,5.80,5.80, 5.56,6.43,6.72,6.81,6.85,6.86,6.87,6.87,6.86,6.85,6.86,6.87, 5.55,7.44,8.64,9.46,10.06,10.56,10.90,11.13,11.33,11.47,11.59,11.69 ), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE ) colnames(AvgLength_bootstrap) <- paste0("h=",1:12) rownames(AvgLength_bootstrap) <- c("ar=0.3","ar=0.6","ar=0.9") AvgLengthBS <- AvgLength_bootstrap ``` ## Result - Coverage ```{r} print(Coverage) # Normal Assumption (Misspecified) print(CoverageBS) # Bootstrapped ```
**Comments:** - One finding to note is that the coverage properties deteriorate for larger $h$ when $\phi_{1}=0.9$. - The finite sample statistical properties of prediction with strong autocorrelation (i.e., large $\phi_{1}$) can require larger samples for the asymptotic properties (i.e. 95% coverage) to apply.
## Result - Lengths ```{r} print(AvgLength) # Normal Assumption (Misspecified) print(AvgLengthBS) # Bootstrapped ```
The average lengths of the prediction intervals increases with $h$ and $\phi_{1}$ (the same applied in part a) $\implies$ Long-horizon prediction is more difficult when time series are more strongly autocorrelated.
## Conclusion - Overall, there is no advantage to be found for the bootstrap intervals in this model. If anything they are slightly longer. - Despite the non-normality, the normal prediction intervals work quite well in this case. - This could be due to the shape of non-normality is different in this case, as the distribution is symmetric. ::: ## {data-background-color="#000F46"}
